# Issue: roboflow/rf-detr #426

- Repository: roboflow/rf-detr | [ICLR 2026] RF-DETR is a real-time object detection and segmentation model architecture developed by Roboflow, SOTA on COCO, designed for fine-tuning. | 6K stars | Python

## RF-DETR + Dynamic Query for small object detection

- Author: [@john09282922](https://github.com/john09282922)
- State: closed (completed)
- Labels: enhancement
- Created: 2025-10-24T22:39:38Z
- Updated: 2026-02-24T14:26:58Z
- Closed: 2026-02-24T14:26:58Z
- Closed by: [@Borda](https://github.com/Borda)

### Search before asking

- [x] I have searched the RF-DETR [issues](https://github.com/roboflow/rf-detr/issues) and found no similar feature requests.

### Description

Adoption of Dynamic Query. I think RF-DETR follows a DETR-style pipeline (backbone → transformer decoder with queries → heads), so the query generator is a modular insertion point. Possible to graft Dynamic Query (DQ) from DQ-DETR—i.e., a per-image adaptive query count and density-guided query initialization—by replacing the fixed query embedding + fixed reference points with a learned counting head + density head that drive per-image query sampling. Decoder, heads, and matching remain compatible after minor masking changes. I am not sure this idea is good for small object detection? what do you think? and it is not effect on inference speed.

### Use case

_No response_

### Additional

_No response_

### Are you willing to submit a PR?

- [ ] Yes I'd like to help by submitting a PR!

---

results.text:
# Suggestions for Small Object Detection

- State: closed
- Author: whittenator
- Created: 2025-04-03T19:49:52Z
- Updated: 2026-02-11T16:10:07Z
- Repository: roboflow/rf-detr
- Number: #112

---

Any suggestions to configuration for detecting objects as small as 5x5 pixels? With YOLOv8 I can add a Pyramid Pooling Layer(P2) that works really well and on top of that using the "mosaic" augmentation additionally helps. Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated.

## Timeline

**isaacrob-roboflow** commented on 2025-04-04T16:07:21Z:

> are you asking about ways to do it within the existing interface or approaches that could be used to modify the model? mosaic and other augmentations also will work with this model, we just don't need them to beat yolo on the metrics we care about so we didn't include them in the repo. you can also upscale your image either during or post training and expect better results on small objects, but that comes with a latency hit.
> 
> can you say a bit more about your goal?

**whittenator** commented on 2025-04-04T16:46:21Z:

> > are you asking about ways to do it within the existing interface or approaches that could be used to modify the model? mosaic and other augmentations also will work with this model, we just don't need them to beat yolo on the metrics we care about so we didn't include them in the repo. you can also upscale your image either during or post training and expect better results on small objects, but that comes with a latency hit.
> > 
> > can you say a bit more about your goal?
> 
> The goal is to use this in a production Nvidia Deepstream application on real-time RTSP video streams from PTZ cameras. Currently we are using YOLOv8 from Ultralytics but we want to steer away from using anything Ultralytics as their AGPL-3.0 license puts the models we generate into a gray area and we aren't allowed to share the training code. Uses for our model are to detect small flying objects such as drones or birds as well as larger targets such as vehicles/humans. Because we are using PTZ cameras, the model needs to be able to handle multiscale objects. Our current application will detect objects(YoloV8), automatically take control of the PTZ camera to start tracking the object and then it will auto zoom in to get enough pixels on target where a secondary image classifier(EfficientNet) will classify the type of object(multi-rotor, bird, fixed-wing, truck, car, human). The model is used on both EO(Color) and IR cameras(SWIR,MWIR,LWIR) and works well enough but we like the license of RF-DETR. As an example, we get a radar hit on a target, slew the camera and it will be small like so(16x12 pixels):
> Image
> 
> The Nvidia Deepstream application will automatically take control of the PTZ camera and start to track and zoom in to get enough pixels(24x16 pixels):
> Image
> 
> Once enough pixels are on target the algorithm will try to maintain the amount of pixels until it get's a solid classification(37x23 pixels):
> Image
> 
> Unfortunately we aren't able to use any slicing techniques, like SAHI, as we have a real-time requirement and slicing is too compute intensive. Thus, we are looking for a model architecture that can handle very small(5x5 pixels to 10x10 pixels) to large scales of objects. Any tips or tricks for training RF-DETR to achieve this would be greatly appreciated.

**isaacrob-roboflow** commented on 2025-04-04T17:06:07Z:

> neat! 
> 
> what size yolo are you using and at what resolution? 
> 
> there's some reason to believe that DETR detectors in general are particularly weak on small objects, and we run our detector at a lower resolution which may compound that. you can of course run ours at a higher resolution but you'll get a latency hit.
> 
> it may be that our model is not a good fit for you but this seems like a fairly niche case and a good opportunity to optimize our model. have you tried training an rf-detr yet?

**whittenator** commented on 2025-04-04T19:20:01Z:

> > neat!
> > 
> > what size yolo are you using and at what resolution?
> > 
> > there's some reason to believe that DETR detectors in general are particularly weak on small objects, and we run our detector at a lower resolution which may compound that. you can of course run ours at a higher resolution but you'll get a latency hit.
> > 
> > it may be that our model is not a good fit for you but this seems like a fairly niche case and a good opportunity to optimize our model. have you tried training an rf-detr yet?
> 
> We are using a few different resolutions of YOLOv8-P2(768x768, 1024x1024, and 1280x1280). Depending on the hardware available we are using nano(n), small(s) and medium(m) sized models. For our embedded Jetson deployments we are using nano or small and for server(A40/L40) deployments medium models. It also depends on the resolution of the PTZ camera modules(as an example we have a Thermal/Visible PTZ unit that outputs 768x576 for all 3 of it's cameras(EO/MWIR/SWIR) and we use the 768x768 sized model). We are able to use these higher resolutions and sizes by converting to TensorRT with FP16/INT8 precision with minimal hits to accuracy to achieve real-time. 
> 
> The Deformable DETR developers were able to enhance the DETR architecture to be able to handle small objects(https://github.com/fundamentalvision/Deformable-DETR), but it's rather compute intensive.
> 
> I haven't tried training yet an RF-DETR model, wanted to first ask the small object detection question before deep diving. My first thoughts are to augment that dataset using Mosaic to see if that helps after doing a base model training. 

**isaacrob-roboflow** commented on 2025-04-05T20:13:41Z:

> we use deformable attention :) it's less compute intensive with modern model compilation. 
> 
> try it and see what happens! the rf-detr base at 560 should be similar runtime to yolov8m at 640, we're hoping to release faster variants soon. curious how it does!

**BotaoPeng98** commented on 2025-04-07T06:43:16Z:

> Hi! Travis, I have experimented with RF-DETR on small object detection. RF-DETR's performance is better! Especially on those occasions that the objects' scale differs or some objects are missing by annotators. 
> 
> The architectures of YOLO I used for comparison are YOLOv11n and YOLOV8 with P2 variant. Due to confidentiality concerns, I can not show you my results, but I highly recommend you train an RF-DETR model on your own datasets and determine whether it works on your application.

- RolandasRazma subscribed

**robmarkcole** commented on 2025-05-07T12:42:56Z:

> Perhaps all that is required here is documentation/tutorial on selecting the best parameters to achieve good performance on small objects. I'm interested in objects that could be as small as 2x2 pixels - somehow I would be interested in an arg `mean_pixels` which would lead to the selection of the optimum parameters for targets of that size. I guess this might become a workflow on Roboflow

**isaacrob-roboflow** commented on

# Accuracy Drop While Trying to Detect Moving Objects

- State: open
- Author: AC-20261
- Created: 2026-04-01T18:28:17Z
- Updated: 2026-04-14T14:35:16Z
- Repository: roboflow/rf-detr
- Number: #906

## Labels

- question

---

Hi,
I trained a RFDETRMedium object detection model to detect some objects, and one of them are some metal rods.
My image sizes are 1920x1080 and I have trained it for 100 epochs. I have trained with an without blur and motion blur augmentations from roboflow.

The results are good, but when someone moves the rod, the rod gets blurred a bit (Still somewhat clearly visible). At these points, the detections are not proper and is not getting detected properly.
I have added images of rods that are moving also for training, but still no improvement. Could someone advise me on how to proceed for better detections of moving objects. Should I :

1) Resize the whole image to model input resolution (576x576) before training
2)Crop the images to 640x640 and give to training
Or is there any other proper way?

Also, I was inferring with the following link:
https://rfdetr.roboflow.com/latest/learn/run/detection/#run-on-video-webcam-or-rtsp-stream

Here, the frame is converted to RGB using
frame_rgb = cv2.cvtColor(frame_bgr, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)

Is this step necessary or can we directly give frame_bgr?

## Timeline

**isaacrob** commented on 2026-04-01T20:31:17Z:

> I'd recommend adjusting the exposure on your camera to reduce motion blur

**AC-20261** commented on 2026-04-02T03:28:53Z:

> I have tried that also. I tried increasing the shutter speed of the camera. Improvement is there, but still it does not get detected properly

- Borda added label "question"

**S-Mahoney** commented on 2026-04-11T12:46:41Z:

> This could be a problem with the dinov2 feature extractor as opposed to the RFDETR model, as movement blur causes important features of an object to disappear. To confirm this you could do an experiment and visualise outputs of pure Dinov2 to see if the object is still somewhat identifiable during movement frames. 

**AC-20261** commented on 2026-04-13T20:45:31Z:

> Hi. I tried this. So when I did this with size 224x224 input size for Dinov2, the object in motion was not that clear. But when i increase the input size, the object in motion is much more clearer

**S-Mahoney** commented on 2026-04-13T21:06:57Z:

> You could also try cropping your original image into 224x224 sections, then it wont do any downscaling on the input

**isaacrob** commented on 2026-04-14T14:35:16Z:

> Honestly I think the best thing here is to increase the amount of training images that show blur or reduce the presence of blur at test time. If those are satisfied I don't really know of any reason it wouldn't work. 
> 
> How many blur images do you have in the train set vs non blur?

results.title: Clarification on num_queries, num_select, and max_dets (small-instance segmentation appears capped / missing)
results.text:
# Clarification on num_queries, num_select, and max_dets (small-instance segmentation appears capped / missing)

- State: closed
- Author: cyh5757
- Created: 2026-02-12T05:46:35Z
- Updated: 2026-02-23T04:47:30Z
- Repository: roboflow/rf-detr
- Number: #669

---

Hi RF-DETR team, thanks for the project.

I’m training RF-DETR for instance segmentation on a microscopy cell dataset where many objects are very small(also has big cell). During inference, I’m seeing that small instances are frequently missing from the predictions, and it feels like there may be a bottleneck related to query selection / postprocessing limits.

## What I’m observing
- Many small cell instances that are present in the GT are not predicted (even when I lower the confidence threshold - ex: 0.01).
- In some images, it looks like the output count might be effectively capped (or biased toward larger / higher-score instances).

## Setup (for reproducibility)
- Task: Instance Segmentation
- Model: 2XL
- Image size / train resolution: 1024 -> 768
- Dataset: Microscopy cells (small objects), COCO-style masks
- Inference settings:
 - conf threshold: 0.01

## Questions
1) Could you explain what each of these means in RF-DETR’s pipeline (especially for segmentation)?
 - num_queries : does this represent the number of object queries fed into the decoder (upper bound on candidate instances)?
 - num_select : is this the number of queries kept after scoring (top-k) before mask generation / postprocess?
 - maxDets : is this the final cap on the number of detections returned/evaluated per image?

2) For small-instance-heavy datasets, what is the recommended way to increase recall?
 - Which parameter is the correct one to change to allow more candidate instances to survive to the final output?

3) Is there any known limitation where the model effectively can’t exceed ~500 predictions per image (or similar), even if I set maxDets=500?

If helpful, I can share:
- a few example images with GT vs prediction overlays
- per-image prediction count distributions
- the exact command line / config dump

Thanks in advance!

## Timeline

- frittatelle subscribed

**SebastianJanampa** commented on 2026-02-17T03:22:22Z:

> Hi,
> RF-DETR is trained using the DINO-DETR mixing strategy, in which positional queries (box coordinates) are initialized from the encoder's feature maps. On the other hand, content queries are initialized using learnable queries (you will update these queries/vectors after every iteration during training). That's why the limit is 500 (although I think it is 300 according to the paper). You can reduce the number of queries, but not increase it, since new queries would be random inputs and could harm the model rather than improve it. 
> 
> I can give you two pieces of advice: 1) check how many cells you have to detect per image. If you have more than the number of queries, then, unfortunately, you can't directly use RF-DETR, and 2) how small the cells are. That's quite important because DETR models do not outperform for small objects (yet). One solution is to crop the image into small subimages, train RF-DETR on those, and during inference use SAHI+RF-DETR. 

**isaacrob** commented on 2026-02-17T16:19:35Z:

> num_queries gives the max detectable number of objects and due to pretraining is 300. num_select is the number of results returned from the model. maxDets is the number of predictions considered when computing mAP. 
> 
> Don't think there's a reason to believe there's a fundamental issue with small objects. In our paper when controlling for latency we exceeded the baselines on small objects on COCO, and we haven't run head to heads on datasets with extremely small objects. 
> 
> Due to an architectural bottleneck, the segmentation model has an upper bound on the number of objects it can detect that is different from num_queries. Specifically, it is 256, and accuracy may degrade as that limit is approached. Any updates we make in the future to the segmentation model will likely address this bottleneck. Note that it is not present in the detector. 

**cyh5757** commented on 2026-02-23T04:45:25Z:

> @SebastianJanampa 
> Thanks for the detailed explanation — it was really helpful. I’m working on very small cells/instances, and I confirmed the model can localize small objects with high confidence, but as you said the hard cap on the number of queries becomes the bottleneck, so it can’t produce more detections beyond that.
> I also tried fine-tuning only the query-related part to increase the number of queries, but I could only push it from ~200 to at most ~300, and the GPU cost went up a lot.
> In the end, I switched to SAHI + RF-DETR as you suggested. It’s inevitably slower, but it does give me the results I need. Next, I’m planning to train with a SAHI-style window/slice size as well. Thanks again!

- SebastianJanampa mentioned

- SebastianJanampa subscribed

**cyh5757** commented on 2026-02-23T04:47:30Z:

> @isaacrob 
> Thanks — you were right that the model’s performance itself wasn’t the problem. It turned out to be an architectural limitation.
> 
> I had seen a post where someone tried to address the num_queries limitation by training from scratch, and I was curious about how they approached it. So I ran my own experiment: I increased num_queries, unfroze only the modules related to num_queries, and froze the rest during training. I was able to push past the cap, but the results didn’t improve accordingly (likely because my dataset is relatively small). Still, it helped me reach a clear conclusion: the model isn’t fundamentally flawed, and there is a capped limit/bottleneck in the segmentation architecture.
> 
> At the moment I’m applying SAHI as suggested in another reply, and I’m getting satisfactory results. If you come across (or can share) a solid “from scratch” approach to address this limitation, I’d really appreciate it.

- cyh5757 closed

- isaacrob mentioned

- isaacrob subscribed

- lwdevelop191 subscribed

# Issue: roboflow/rf-detr #203

- Repository: roboflow/rf-detr | [ICLR 2026] RF-DETR is a real-time object detection and segmentation model architecture developed by Roboflow, SOTA on COCO, designed for fine-tuning. | 6K stars | Python

## RF-DETR not detecting more than 300 objects

- Author: [@emerson-w](https://github.com/emerson-w)
- State: closed (completed)
- Labels: bug
- Created: 2025-05-08T15:37:10Z
- Updated: 2026-02-24T14:20:57Z
- Closed: 2026-02-24T14:20:57Z
- Closed by: [@Borda](https://github.com/Borda)

I am installing RFDETR directly from the source using:
pip install git+https://github.com/roboflow/rf-detr.git

And training like so:

```py
model = RFDETRBase()
model.train(
    dataset_dir='...',
    num_queries = 700,
    num_select = 700
)
```

I'm getting this runtime error.

```
RuntimeError                              Traceback (most recent call last)
<ipython-input-18-23f754c7ec85> in <cell line: 0>()
     18 model = RFDETRBase()
     19 
---> 20 model.train(
     21     dataset_dir='/content/drive/MyDrive/RMMC_CAN_ds_v3/images',
     22     num_queries = 700,

7 frames
/usr/local/lib/python3.11/dist-packages/rfdetr/models/lwdetr.py in forward(self, outputs, target_sizes)
    552 
    553         prob = out_logits.sigmoid()
--> 554         topk_values, topk_indexes = torch.topk(prob.view(out_logits.shape[0], -1), self.num_select, dim=1)
    555         scores = topk_values
    556         topk_boxes = topk_indexes // out_logits.shape[2]

RuntimeError: selected index k out of range
```

Is it possible to train RF-DETR to detect more than 300 images? How can I do this?

---

### Timeline

**@isaacrob-roboflow** commented · May 12, 2025 at 9:18pm

> unfortunately, using the pretrained checkpoint you won't be able to detect more than 300 objects in a given image. you'd have to train from scratch.
> 
> can you say a bit more about your use case?

**@emerson-w** commented · May 13, 2025 at 6:05pm · Author · edited

> I am now training from scratch like so:
> 
> ```py
> model = RFDETRBase(
> pretrain_weights=None, 
> num_classes=1,
> num_queries =700,
> num_select = 700
> )
> 
> model.train(
> dataset_dir= '...',
> num_queries = 700,

> epochs=100,
> ...
> )
> 
> detections = model.predict(image, threshold=0.1, num_select = 700, num_queries = 700)

> 
> But there are still only 300 detections. Is it possible for RF-DETR to predict more than 300 objects?
> 
> My use case is counting the number of small objects in an image. These objects are all similar (num_classes = 1) and the training data supports this large number. I would like to be able to identify more than 300 objects without splitting up the image.

**@isaacrob-roboflow** commented · May 14, 2025 at 4:45pm

> that is likely a bug :) probably the num_select argument isn't getting propagated correctly .. are you comfortable submitting a PR?

**@Rookiehhh** commented · Jun 25, 2025 at 7:25am

> There is a bug in the code, at line 94 in main.py:
> 
> ```python
> checkpoint_num_classes = checkpoint['model']['class_embed.bias'].shape[0]
> if checkpoint_num_classes != args.num_classes + 1:
> logger.warning(
> f"num_classes mismatch: pretrain weights has {checkpoint_num_classes - 1} classes, but your model has {args.num_classes} classes\n"
> f"reinitializing detection head with {checkpoint_num_classes - 1} classes"
> )
> self.reinitialize_detection_head(checkpoint_num_classes)
> ```
> 
> The num_class is forcibly aligned with the pretrained weights, but it should be set to match the number of classes in your own dataset.
> 
> ```python
> checkpoint_num_classes = checkpoint['model']['class_embed.bias'].shape[0]
> if checkpoint_num_classes != args.num_classes + 1:
> logger.warning(
> f"num_classes mismatch: pretrain weights has {checkpoint_num_classes - 1} classes, but your model has {args.num_classes} classes\n"
> f"reinitializing detection head with {args.num_classes} classes"
> )
> self.reinitialize_detection_head(args.num_classes + 1) # HACK: The original code writes checkpoint_num_classes here, but it should actually be checkpoint_num_classes
> # HACK: When loading the model, we need to crop class_embed.weight and class_embed.bias to args.num_classes + 1
> for key in checkpoint['model'].keys():
> if 'class_embed' in key:
> checkpoint['model'][key] = checkpoint['model'][key][:args.num_classes + 1]
> ```

> The above is my approach, but it only considers cases where the number of classes is fewer than in the model file. If there are more classes, please try random reinitialization or other methods. I tried random initialization, but the model had excessively large loss values during the initial training phase, causing numerical instability. Although warmup can alleviate this situation to some extent, it is recommended to choose appropriate initialization.

## README

# RF-DETR: Real-Time SOTA Object Detection, Instance Segmentation, and Keypoint Detection

 

version

---

RF-DETR is a real-time transformer architecture for object detection, instance segmentation, and keypoint detection (preview) developed by Roboflow. Built on a DINOv2 vision transformer backbone, RF-DETR delivers state-of-the-art accuracy and latency trade-offs on Microsoft COCO and RF100-VL.

RF-DETR uses a DINOv2 vision transformer backbone and supports object detection, instance segmentation, and keypoint detection (preview) in a single, consistent API. The open-source `rfdetr` package and Apache-designated models are released under Apache 2.0, while Plus components (`rfdetr_plus`, including RF-DETR-XL/2XL detection models) are licensed under PML 1.0.

The published RF-DETR sizes were created with neural architecture search (NAS) — and the same NAS method is now available on the Roboflow platform, so you can discover the best architecture for your own dataset. Learn more in the NAS docs.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/add23fd1-266f-4538-8809-d7dd5767e8e6

## Install

To install RF-DETR, install the `rfdetr` package in a **Python>=3.10** environment with `pip`.

```bash
pip install rfdetr
```

 
 Install from source 

 

By installing RF-DETR from source, you can explore the most recent features and enhancements that have not yet been officially released. **Please note that these updates are still in development and may not be as stable as the latest published release.**

```bash
pip install https://github.com/roboflow/rf-detr/archive/refs/heads/develop.zip
```

 

## Benchmarks

RF-DETR achieves state-of-the-art results in both object detection and instance segmentation, with benchmarks reported on Microsoft COCO and RF100-VL (RF100-VL for detection only). The charts and tables below compare RF-DETR against other top real-time models across accuracy and latency for detection and segmentation. All latency numbers were measured on an NVIDIA T4 using TensorRT, FP16, and batch size 1. For full benchmarking methodology and reproducibility details, see roboflow/sab.
